9.text: Sacrifice to the Young Moon. — Many people offer sacrifices every

10.text: month to the young moon. The offering consists of blood-soup, meat, and

11.text: tallow, also of small figures of reindeer made of snow or of leaf-pudding, and

12.text: is made in the evening. Slaughtering is rare, and happens only in midwinter.

13.text: These sacrifices are evidently directed to the evil spirits: therefore they are

14.text: not regarded as belonging to the general cycle of ceremonials. The people,

15.text: when talking about such ceremonials, persist in thinking that they are not

16.text: quite lawful, and should be kept secret.

26.text: Sacrifice for Luck in Hunting. — A man, when going alone into a

27.text: strange country to hunt, or to a lake or river to fish, will offer to the place

28.text: a small sacrifice from his scanty provisions. On the land he will throw the

29.text: offering about; on the river or lake he will throw it into the water.

30.text: After a successful hunt of one of the larger animals. — such as the wolf

31.text: or wolverene, black and polar bear, wild reindeer, walrus, and thong-seal, —

32.text: various ceremonials are performed when the game is brought home. Their

33.text: common feature is the “giving of a drink and a bed” to the animals. This

34.text: is symbolized by bringing out of the house a small quantity of water, and

35.text: pouring it over the head of the animal as it lies on the snow before the

36.text: entrance,¹ and by placing a small willow-twig under the hind-quarters of the

38.text: The Maritime Chukchee also “give a drink” to all larger animals killed

39.text: on the hunt, especially to the walrus; but the “bed” — that is, the willow-twig

40.text: put under the hind-quarters of the animal — is often omitted. The Asiatic

41.text: Eskimo, however, “give a drink” only to the first-killed walrus of the season.
